recorded: 15 March and 18 April 1921, Camden, New Jersey; issued take: 18 April
intro: Stokowski and the Philadelphia Orchestra fit Finlandia onto one twelve-inch record side. The great hymn survives the shortening: a broad tune at the heart of the brass fanfares.

sections.label: A · The march and fanfares
sections.mNote: Quick orchestral phrases before the hymn

sections.label: B · The hymn in A♭ major
sections.mNote: A broad melody replaces the short fanfares

sections.label: C · Fanfares around the hymn
sections.mNote: The closing passage brings the fanfares back

cues.title: Stokowski in Camden
cues.text: On 18 April 1921, Stokowski and the Philadelphia Orchestra return to Victor’s studio in Camden, New Jersey. Their fourth take of Finlandia becomes the issued record. Victor marks the other three takes for destruction.
cues.evidence: Discography of American Historical Recordings, Victor matrix C-24988: two takes on 15 March and two on 18 April 1921; take 4 is the master issued as Victor 74698, the others marked Destroy. https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/matrix/refer/700010224

cues.title: A theatre full of protest
cues.text: At Helsinki’s Swedish Theatre in November 1899, actors present scenes from Finland’s history to raise money for journalists. Russian censorship hangs over the celebrations. Sibelius’s music ends with Finland Awakens, the piece he will revise into Finlandia.
cues.evidence: Sibelius Society of Finland, history of the 1899 Press Celebrations: Swedish Theatre, journalists’ pension fund, censorship, and the final tableau Finland Awakens. https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_finlandia.htm

cues.title: The hymn without words
cues.text: The hymn unfolds in A♭ major, its long phrases a release from the short fanfares. Sibelius writes it for the orchestra. The familiar Finnish words arrive much later, when V. A. Koskenniemi supplies a text in 1940.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, p. 17, rehearsal I, reproduced in the Sibelius Society of Finland’s account; the same account dates Koskenniemi’s text and its first performance to 1940. https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_finlandia.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Fanfares around the hymn
cues.text: The closing passage brings the fanfares back around the hymn. Its broad tune can stand against the quicker figures without hurrying. Sibelius carries both towards the final orchestral chords.
cues.evidence: Sibelius Society of Finland describes the faster closing passage, returning brass fanfares and continued hymn. The abridgement’s individual cuts and revised orchestration are undocumented. https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_finlandia.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: DAHR gives Philadelphia Orchestra and Leopold Stokowski. The Internet Archive item credits “Philadelphia Symphony Orchestra”, a variant of the same ensemble’s name. DAHR’s instrumentation list (7 first violins, 5 second violins, 3 violas, 2 cellos, 4 basses, harp, 3 oboes, 3 clarinets, 2 bassoons, 2 trumpets, 3 trombones, 2 tubas, traps) comes from Victor ledgers for 15 March 1921 and is not confirmed for the issued take.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Abridged orchestral version; which passages are omitted is not documented
fields.note: The abridgement is inferred from the file’s length, 4:06, against a typical performance of 7½–9 minutes (Wikipedia), and from the disc being a single 12-inch side. DAHR and the Internet Archive do not describe the cut, and neither names an edition or cut scheme. This dossier does not locate cut bars.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.value: 18 April 1921 (issued take 4); earlier takes 1–2 on 15 March 1921
fields.note: DAHR: takes 1 and 2 on 15 March 1921 and 3 on 18 April were destroyed; take 4 (18 April 1921) is the issued master. A bracketed [1921] is the date given for the issue on Victor 74698. Some listings give the earlier date for the first takes.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: DAHR gives Camden, New Jersey for every take.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: DAHR describes the object as Victor 74698, Red Seal 12-inch single-faced. Later issues on Victor 6366 and Gramophone Company DB-599 and 3-0662 are listed for the same matrix and take.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The Internet Archive item also shows matrix and catalogue number 74698 and publisher “Victrola”.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: The Internet Archive item shows 74698 as its matrix number; the Victor matrix is C-24988.

fields.value: George Blood, L.P. (digitisation (scanning centre), Great 78 Project)
fields.note: The item metadata names George Blood, L.P. as scanning centre and credits Robert Boggs with metadata and transfer entry and Kevin Coupe with cleaning (as Internet Archive user fields).

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The item’s public date is 19 March 2021; that is the upload date, not a transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Digitised at 78 rpm with four styli (3.8, 2.3, 2.8 and 3.3 mil truncated conical); the preferred version was selected by an engineer at George Blood and copied to the friendly file name
fields.note: The item’s notes say the record was acoustic and that the other side was “not completed due to physical condition of disc”. The MP3 used here is the Internet Archive derivative of the 24-bit FLAC; no further processing is disclosed.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Sibelius died in 1957; in countries with a life-plus-70 term the composition remains in copyright until the end of 2027
fields.note: Computed from the composer’s life dates, given in DAHR’s MARC record as 1865–1957. The composition’s status in other territories is not assessed. The programme’s rule applies to the sound recording.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 2 — United States public domain: first published in 1921, before the 1926 cut-off.
fields.note: DAHR records the issue on Victor 74698 as [1921]; the brackets mean the year was supplied by the cataloguer, and no month of issue is recorded. The take issued was made on 18 April 1921, so publication followed that date. The Internet Archive item date is also 1921. The item has no licence URL and no non-commercial restriction in its metadata.

composer.born: 8 December 1865, Hämeenlinna, Grand Duchy of Finland
composer.epithet: He watched sixteen swans circle over Ainola, gave their flight to the horns, and spent four years getting the Fifth Symphony right.
facts: Wegelius in Helsinki, 1885–89; Becker in Berlin; Fuchs and Goldmark in Vienna
Ainola, Lars Sonck’s timber house near Lake Tuusula, from 1904
Swedish at home; Finnish at school and in Kullervo and Luonnotar
Seven symphonies, one violin concerto, tone poems, theatre music, songs and chamber music
composer.background:
In Vienna in 1891, Sibelius auditioned for the Philharmonic and failed. He wanted to be a violinist; the jury found him too nervous even for an orchestral post. He was twenty-five, studying composition with Robert Fuchs and Karl Goldmark, spending money he did not have at parties and taking in as much music as the city could offer. After hearing Bruckner’s Third Symphony he thought its author the greatest living composer. Meanwhile, in his lodgings, he was studying the rhythms of the Finnish Kalevala.

He had been born in Hämeenlinna in 1865, when Finland was a grand duchy of the Russian Empire. His father, a doctor, died three years later, leaving debts. At home the family spoke Swedish; at school Janne learnt Finnish. He played chamber music with his sister Linda and brother Christian, and in 1885 went to Helsinki, nominally to study law. Martin Wegelius’s Music Institute soon claimed his days. There he befriended Ferruccio Busoni and worked through quartets by Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven. His professional name came cheaply: he found a dead uncle’s visiting cards. “Jean is now my musical name,” he told Uncle Pehr on 31 March 1886. Studies with Albert Becker in Berlin followed Helsinki, then came Vienna.
